analysis.one_liner: Gives crypto trading platforms a safe harbor from SEC enforcement when listing digital tokens.
analysis.headline: A bill to shield crypto exchanges from SEC enforcement for listing digital tokens died in committee with no cosponsors and no Senate vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have set up a legal 'safe harbor' for crypto exchanges and other intermediaries. If a digital token had not been officially declared a security by the SEC or a court, an exchange that met certain listing, custody, and disclosure rules could list it without facing SEC enforcement for trading an unregistered security. Even if a token was later ruled a security, the exchange would get a two-year window during which the SEC could not pursue certain enforcement actions against it.
analysis.who_benefits: Crypto exchanges and other trading platforms gain the most: they could list a wide range of digital tokens without registering as broker-dealers or securities exchanges, and even a token later deemed a security would come with a two-year shield from SEC enforcement over the listing. Token issuers would also gain, because their assets could trade freely unless the SEC or a court affirmatively ruled them to be securities.

how_it_helps.text: An intermediary that meets requirements on listing processes, private-key custody, anti-money-laundering controls, and risk disclosures would be able to treat any token not yet ruled a security as not being a security, avoiding securities-law enforcement for listing it.

If the SEC or a court determines a token is a security, an intermediary that met the requirements gets a two-year compliance period in which the SEC may not pursue enforcement over the listing or over failure to register as a broker-dealer or exchange, with transactions routed through a registered bank or broker-dealer after 180 days.

The intermediary could even go to court for a declaration that the token is not a security, notwithstanding an SEC determination, and the court could let it keep listing the token while the case is pending.
If the SEC first called a token a security and later reversed itself, the intermediary would be shielded from enforcement for having listed it in the meantime.

analysis.who_pays: Investors who buy tokens on these platforms would bear the added risk. Under the bill's default, a token is treated as not a security unless the SEC or a court says otherwise — the opposite of how securities law usually works — so buyers could lose the registration, disclosure, and liability protections that come with securities status. The bill itself requires exchanges to warn customers that investor protections like SIPC coverage do not apply to non-security digital assets.

drawbacks.text: The bill reverses the usual burden: rather than an issuer or exchange having to show a token is not a security, the token is treated as not a security unless the SEC or a court affirmatively determines otherwise, weakening the default investor protections of securities law.

Even after a token is determined to be a security, the exchange gets a two-year enforcement shield, meaning investors could be buying an unregistered security for two years without the usual remedies against the platform.

Customer protections are weaker than securities registration: the bill requires exchanges to disclose that SIPC investor protection does not apply to non-security digital assets, so customers are left thinner safeguards than stock buyers have.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would have given crypto exchanges the legal clarity they asked for, and it did carry real obligations — custody controls, anti-money-laundering programs, risk disclosures, and a requirement to route trades through regulated banks or broker-dealers during a transition. But its central trade tilts toward the industry: the default assumption that tokens are not securities, plus a two-year shield even after a security determination, moves risk from platforms onto the people buying the tokens. Weighing it honestly, the consumer protections in the text are narrower than what securities registration would have required, and the people asked to absorb the risk are ordinary investors, not the exchanges.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Banking Committee, which never acted on it, so it died when the Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Sen. Bill Hagerty introduced the bill on September 29, 2022, near the end of the 117th Congress, with no cosponsors.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs, which took no further action on it.
The bill never received a committee vote or a floor vote, and it expired when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, the existing securities-law framework stayed intact: the SEC kept its full authority over token listings, and crypto exchanges remained exposed to enforcement rather than gaining a two-year shield. Retail investors were spared a default rule that would have treated most tokens as unregulated assets.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The SEC's enforcement authority, and token buyers

for.name: Sen. Bill Hagerty
for.role: U.S. Senator from Tennessee; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and got it read twice and referred to the Banking Committee.

against.name: Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee
against.what_they_did: Never acted on the bill after referral — no hearing, markup, or vote — letting it die at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No cosponsors joined and no votes were ever taken, so the record shows only a single Republican sponsor and no measurable partisan split.

industries.industry: Crypto exchanges and digital asset trading platforms
industries.note: The bill would have freed them from SEC registration and enforcement over token listings, shifting that risk onto their customers, while also imposing custody, anti-money-laundering, and disclosure obligations they do not currently face as a package. Their core gain — avoiding securities registration — comes at the cost of investor protections.

industries.industry: Token issuers and crypto project sponsors
industries.note: Their tokens could trade freely on compliant platforms unless the SEC or a court ruled them securities, making it easier to raise money from the public without registering offerings. Investors buying those tokens would lack the disclosures and remedies registration provides.

The bill required exchanges to route transactions through a registered bank or broker-dealer during compliance periods, with net capital and customer-funds safeguarding rules, creating paid business for these firms.

The bill would have stripped the SEC of enforcement tools over token listings, forced it to treat undeclared tokens as non-securities by default, and limited its ability to act for two years even after a security determination.
